# rasuvaeff/understudy-phpstan

PHPStan extension for `rasuvaeff/understudy`.

## Install

```bash
composer require --dev rasuvaeff/understudy-phpstan
```

With `phpstan/extension-installer` that is all. Without it:

```neon
includes:
    - vendor/rasuvaeff/understudy-phpstan/extension.neon
```

Namespace: `Rasuvaeff\Understudy\PhpStan`. Requires PHP 8.3 - 8.5,
`phpstan/phpstan ^2.2.2` and `rasuvaeff/understudy ^0.4 || ^0.5 || ^0.6 || ^0.7`.

## API

There is none. The extension's whole surface is `extension.neon` and the
error identifiers below — every class it registers is `@internal`, and a
project never names one.

## Rules

- A matcher is typed `never`, the bottom type every parameter accepts. That
  is why `Arg::int()` may stand in for a declared `int` at level 9+ — and why
  NOTHING is suppressed: a wrong argument beside the matcher, an undefined
  method on the double, and the statements around the closure all keep their
  reports.
- `Arg::rest()` (understudy 0.4) legitimately passes fewer arguments than the
  contract declares: the `arguments.count` report is ignored wherever a
  call's last written argument is `Arg::rest()`. In a real call the line is
  reported once, as `understudy.matcherLeak` — the leak is the actual
  mistake, and the engine answers the call with `ArgumentCountError`.
- `$captor->capture()` (understudy 0.4, `Arg::captor()`) is a matcher too:
  typed `never` when the receiver is a `Captor` (a foreign `capture()` is
  left alone), not counted against "exactly one call per closure", and
  reported by `understudy.matcherLeak` in a real call. `Arg::captor()` itself
  is a factory, not a matcher, and lives outside the closure.
- The matcher's own kind is NOT encoded in that type on purpose. Typing
  `Arg::string()` as `string` would make a `non-empty-string` parameter an
  error, and a matcher can match a non-empty string. Impossible pairings are
  reported by a rule instead, which asks whether ANY value of the kind fits
  and stays silent on "maybe".
- `when()` / `expect()` get the builder type they really produce, so
  `returns()` and `answers()` are checked against the method being specified
  rather than against `mixed`. Left alone when the method returns `void`,
  `never` or `mixed`: `WhenBuilder<void>` is a claim nobody can satisfy.
- `Understudy::wire(Sut::class)` gets the shape read off the constructor. An
  intersection parameter is one double and keeps the intersection; a union
  naming two object types makes the core refuse the class (`CannotWire`), so
  no shape is produced for that call at all. A dynamic class-string is left
  alone.
- Both spellings are understood: the free functions a test file imports
  (`when()`, `expect()`, `expectSequence()`, `verify()`) and the `Understudy::`
  static form Pest users reach for, plus the readers that have no function
  spelling — `calls()`, `lastCall()`, `verifySequence()`.
- No baseline, no ignored errors of our own. Rules stay silent whenever they
  are not sure.

## Identifiers

- `understudy.closure` — the closure specifies nothing, makes more than one
  call, or calls a static method a double cannot intercept.
- `understudy.cardinality` — `times(5, 2)`, a negative bound,
  `verify(…, never: true, times: 3)`, `times` beside a `minimum`.
- `understudy.matcher` — a matcher whose kind the parameter can never accept.
- `understudy.returns` — `returns()` on a method declared `void`.
- `understudy.matcherLeak` — a matcher written outside a specification, where
  it reaches the code as a value. This one exists BECAUSE matchers are typed
  `never`: without it the extension would be weaker than no extension for
  that mistake.

Silence one with `ignoreErrors: - identifier: understudy.matcherLeak`.

## Levels

- Level 9+: the matcher typing is what makes specifications analysable at all.
- Any level, including 0: the rules, the builder type and the `wire()` shape.
